app.title: Hotel Pixel Simulation
app.rotate: Turn your phone sideways (landscape) for the best view

setup.intro: Run an 8-room hostel for 12 weeks against 3 bot hotels in the same city. Pick a city on the map or with the buttons on the right.
setup.mapCredit: Pixel map traced from real borders ({src})
setup.startMonthHint: 12 weeks ≈ 3 months. The month decides whether the game falls in this city's high or low season.
setup.allowFake: Allow the fake-review strategy (risk of being caught)
setup.seedHint: Use the same code for the whole class: everyone gets the same bots, event calendar and random events.

top.info: Events and how they are drawn

info.title: Info: event library and how events are drawn

end.needStaff: Hire at least 1 front office staff member first (Staff tab)

market.noNews: No news yet. Problems at competing hotels will appear here.
market.calIntro: Scheduled events (festivals, concerts, conferences) are announced in advance, so you can plan prices for them. Emergencies (weather, disasters, politics) are only known after they happen. An announced event has a {p}% chance of being cancelled.

decide.overText: Read the final week's report, then open the summary below.
decide.title: Decisions for week {n}
decide.noEvents: No announced events. Emergencies are only revealed after the week ends.
decide.wtpNote: The nightly budget is what this group is willing to pay on average. Price far above it and they go elsewhere; the higher the price, the more service they expect.
decide.priceNote: The − / + buttons change the price by 50 baht, or click the slider and use the arrow keys for 10-baht steps. Average price for this city's demand ≈ {ref} baht.
decide.closed: {n} rooms closed for repair for {w} more weeks
decide.onlineSub: Works fast, fades fast when you stop
decide.infNote: Influencer results are uncertain. If your real service is poor, your reputation drops.
decide.ota: Sell through OTAs (more people see you; {p}% commission on OTA bookings)
decide.otaBan: Banned from OTAs for {n} more weeks for fake reviews
decide.fakeNote: Stars rise fast, but you can be caught every week: {fine} ฿ fine, stars drop and a 3-week OTA ban. In the real world, {src} bans buying and selling fake reviews.

staff.qualityIntro: Your team's average (coloured bar) vs the competitors' average (black line). Each stat maps to a {src} dimension.
staff.expectNote: Black line = guests' average expectation ({e}). If the bar is shorter than the line, reviews fall below 3.4 stars.
staff.loadNote: Above 30 room-nights per person per week in the same position, staff satisfaction drops.
staff.chartEmpty: The chart appears after the first week.
staff.rolesIntro: Each applicant applies for one position. Service quality = 60% from the front office team + 40% from the housekeeping team. Skills used by each position are in bold.
staff.help_fo: Check-in, information and talking to guests. Uses appearance, service mind, professionalism and languages (languages matter a lot in cities with many foreign guests).
staff.help_hk: Rooms clean and ready as booked. Uses mainly experience, plus service mind. With no housekeeper, front office staff clean instead at 70% quality and twice the workload.
staff.help_fb: Runs the restaurant. Uses service mind, experience and appearance; about 150 diners per person per week. Can be hired once restaurant work starts (Type 2).
staff.noHK: No housekeeper yet: front office staff must clean the rooms

customer.emptyTitle: Customer data appears after the first week
customer.emptyText: This page shows each customer group's awareness, expectations, satisfaction and online reviews (eWOM).
customer.awIntro: Share of each group that knows your hotel (coloured bar) vs the competitors' average (black line), built from accumulated marketing and OTAs.
customer.gapIntro: Coloured bar = service delivered to each group; black line = expectation. The gap between them is the core idea of {src}. The higher the price, the higher the expectation.
customer.satLine: New reviews this week: {newRev} · average this week: {rating} · overall stars {R} from {N} reviews
customer.ewomIntro: eWOM is word of mouth on the internet. It matters a lot for hotels because guests cannot test the service before staying ({src}). The sample reviews below come from real causes in the game.
customer.fakeWarn: Fake reviews are mixed in, so the overall stars are higher than real satisfaction.

pos.serv: Caring staff, great tips on where to go.
pos.value: Good value for money, I'll stay again.
pos.app: Neatly dressed staff, the lobby looks nice.
pos.lang: Staff speak good English, very helpful!
pos.prof: Quick, professional check-in. Good for work trips.
pos.exp: Room was ready as booked, no problems at all.

neg.adequacy: Waited ages to check in, not enough staff.
neg.lang: Hard to communicate, staff barely speak English.
neg.serv: Staff hardly smile and don't seem to want to help.
neg.prof: Not suitable for work trips, my booking details were wrong.
neg.exp: Room wasn't ready at check-in, had to wait for cleaning.

reviews.neu: Okay overall, fair for the price.

report.emptyText: Set prices, hire at least 1 staff member, choose marketing, then press "End week". The game calculates bookings for every hotel at once and explains the result with 4 indicators.
report.headline: Week {week} ({date}): RGI {rgi}, you earned {diff}% {dir} revenue per room than the competitor average
report.bldNote: Lit windows in the building above follow the latest occupancy; red = room closed for repair.
report.quadTitle: Your position: volume × price vs competitors
report.finNote: RevPAR measures room revenue, not profit. A hotel with high RevPAR can still lose money if its costs are high.
report.promptTitle: Question to think about before next week
report.debriefNote: Much of the learning from simulation games happens in the debrief after playing ({src}).
report.guideSummary: Show thinking guide (try answering first, then open)
report.guideNote: This guide is based on the game's rules; it is not the only correct answer.

occ.name: Occupancy
occ.meaning: The share of room-nights sold out of all room-nights available.
occ.why: Shows how much demand reaches your hotel, and drives staff workload and per-room costs.
occ.caution: It ignores price completely: you can cut prices until you are full and still score high. If market demand is low but your rooms are full, your price may be too low.
occ.closed: This week {n} rooms were closed for repair but still count as available.

adr.name: ADR (average daily rate)
adr.meaning: The average price actually achieved per room sold, not the price you set. In this game ADR falls between your weekday and weekend prices, depending on which you sold more of.
adr.why: Measures pricing power. Always read it together with occupancy.
adr.caution: It only counts rooms sold, so a week with few sales at high prices looks better than it is.

revpar.name: RevPAR (revenue per available room)
revpar.meaning: Room revenue averaged over all rooms available, including empty ones.
revpar.why: It combines price and volume in one number, so it tells you whether cutting prices to fill rooms paid off.
revpar.caution: It is not a profit measure and only counts room revenue. See profit in the finance section below.

rgi.name: RGI (RevPAR index vs competitors)
rgi.meaning: Your RevPAR divided by the competitor set's average RevPAR × 100. 100 means you got your fair share of revenue; above 100 is more than expected, below 100 is less.
rgi.breakdown: MPI = occupancy vs competitors, ARI = ADR vs competitors, and RGI = MPI × ARI ÷ 100 {calc}
rgi.why: Every hotel in the city faces the same seasons and events, so RGI measures management skill, not luck.
rgi.caution: What counts as good depends on which competitors you compare with. In this game it is the 3 bot hotels.

quad.yAxis: Y axis: ARI average rate index →
quad.mpi: (Market Penetration Index): your occupancy vs competitors × 100. Above 100 = you sold more than your fair share of rooms.
quad.ari: (Average Rate Index): your ADR vs competitors × 100. Above 100 = you sold at a higher average price than competitors.
quad.dots: Big yellow dot = this week; dashed line = your path in earlier weeks; centre lines = 100

diag.both: You beat competitors on volume (MPI {mpi}) and price (ARI {ari}). Keep this balance and check that your staff can handle the load.
diag.volume: You sold more rooms than competitors (MPI {mpi}) but at a lower average price (ARI {ari}), so you are buying volume with price. Try raising prices a little and see whether RGI improves ({src}).
diag.rate: Your average price is above competitors (ARI {ari}) but you sold less (MPI {mpi}). Check whether your price is above your main customers' budget, or whether awareness and stars are still too low ({src}).
diag.behind: You are behind competitors on volume (MPI {mpi}) and price (ARI {ari}). The problem is usually customer awareness or reputation rather than price.
diag.full: Almost full all week ({occ}), which usually means you can still raise prices ({src}).
diag.weekendGap: Weekends are full ({we}) but weekdays are empty ({wd}). Try a higher weekend price and look for weekday guests such as business travellers.
diag.nextEvent: Next week has {names}, already announced. Try adjusting prices before competitors do, but watch out for cancellations.
diag.understaffed: Not enough staff for the number of guests, so service quality dropped.
diag.language: Your team speaks few foreign languages (average {lang}) in a city with many foreign guests.
diag.commission: OTA commission takes {p} of your room revenue.
diag.lowSat: Staff satisfaction is low ({sat}). Below 40, people start to quit.
diag.negCash: Your cash is negative: you pay 1% interest per week, and hotels with a cumulative loss always rank below profitable hotels.
diag.noHK: No housekeeper: front office staff clean the rooms themselves, so room quality is only about 70% and their workload doubles.

cause.cancelled: The event "{name}" was suddenly cancelled, so the expected demand never came (hotels that raised prices for it lost out).
cause.shock: {arrow} Event "{name}" ({cat}, {phase}{week}): {text} Full effect: {eff} (hits every hotel in the city)
cause.quiet: No events or emergencies this week
cause.price: Your average price {y} ฿ vs competitors {c} ฿ ({d}% {dir})
cause.service: Service delivered {q} vs expectation {e} → this week's reviews {r} stars, overall {R}
cause.infBad: , but guest reviews were below 3 stars so your stars dropped 0.25
cause.fakeCaught: Fake reviews were detected: {fine} ฿ fine, stars −0.7 and a 3-week OTA ban
cause.fakeSafe: Fake reviews were not detected, but the risk is there every week
cause.staff: Front office {nFO} ({lFO} room-nights/person) · Housekeeping {nHK} ({lHK} room-nights/person) · satisfaction {sat}

prompts.q: What drove your sales most this week: price, reputation or customer awareness?
why: Customers first have to "know" your hotel (awareness from accumulated marketing and OTAs); only then do they compare your price with their budget and look at your stars.
If awareness is low, cutting prices won't sell much, because most customers never see your hotel.
If your price is far above your main group's budget, or your stars are below competitors', the customers who do see you choose someone else.
todo: Open the Customers tab and compare the "awareness" bars with the competitor line. If you are far behind, add marketing or turn on OTAs before cutting prices.
Compare your prices with the "nightly budget" of your main customer group in the Decisions tab.
If your stars are low, fix service first (number of staff, workload); overall stars move slowly and take several weeks.

prompts.q: What do your MPI and ARI say about your pricing strategy?
why: High MPI but low ARI: you sell a lot because you are cheaper than competitors, i.e. buying volume with price.
Low MPI but high ARI: your price is higher than customers will pay for your hotel, or not enough customers know you yet.
Both low: the problem is rarely price alone; it is usually awareness or reputation.
todo: The goal is RGI (≈ MPI × ARI ÷ 100), not making either one as high as possible.
Change prices in small steps, e.g. 50–100 baht, and watch which way your dot moves on the 2×2 chart.
If a price rise lowers MPI less than it raises ARI, RGI improves, which means you can still go higher.

prompts.q: This week's event hit every hotel equally. Why did some hotels still get a better RGI?
why: Events reduce demand for the whole city, but each hotel's share still depends on its own price, awareness and stars.
Many events hit some groups harder, such as foreign or business guests; hotels that rely less on those groups suffer less.
Some events raise fixed costs, which hurts profit but not RGI.
todo: Read "Cause → effect" to see which groups the event hit, then check your customer mix in the coloured bar under the building.
When demand drops, set prices that suit the groups still travelling, and cut spending you don't need yet.
Multi-week events are strongest in the first week and then recover; plan to raise prices again in the recovery phase.

prompts.q: Can your staff handle the workload, and how does it affect your reviews?
why: Each person can handle about 30 room-nights per week in their own position (every guest passes the front desk and a room cleaned by housekeeping); above that, satisfaction falls every week.
With too few staff for the number of guests, service quality drops; when it falls below guests' expectations, reviews get worse.
Below 40 satisfaction, people start to quit and the rest carry an even heavier load.
todo: In the Staff tab, check last week's "Workload" bar for each position and "Staffing adequacy".
Hire before busy periods you expect, such as high season or event weeks.
Bonuses lift satisfaction but cost money; weigh them against the better reviews.
Put people where their skills count: good linguists at the front desk, experienced people in housekeeping, and never leave housekeeping empty.

prompts.q: Which segment stayed with you most? Does it match the strategy you planned?
why: Your price selects your customers: each group has a different nightly budget, low prices attract backpackers, high prices leave only the higher-budget groups.
Marketing channels reach groups differently: online ads and influencers reach backpackers and couples well, billboards reach few backpackers but last long.
Groups stay at different times: some mostly on weekdays, others mostly at weekends.
todo: Compare the coloured bar under the building with the customer table in the Decisions tab.
To win a group, price close to its budget and pick marketing channels that reach it.
The higher your price against the budget, the more service guests expect; your team needs the skills that group values.

prompts.q: If you could go back to the start of the week, which decision would you change, and which indicator would you expect to move?
why: Each week's result comes from several decisions at once; working out which one caused what is where you learn the most.
Some decisions show results immediately (price, online ads), others slowly (billboards, star rating).
todo: Change only 1–2 things per week so you can tell what moved the numbers.
Make a prediction before ending the week, e.g. "raise price by 100 baht: Occ should fall but ADR and RGI should rise", then compare with the result.
Check the "Compared with competitors" table to see how competitors changed their prices in the same week.

prompts.q: Have you used the event calendar to set prices in advance? How did it go?
why: Announced events raise demand from some groups; hotels that priced for them in advance earn more per room.
But city events can be cancelled ({cancel}%), and pricing far above competitors in an event week can get you criticised for price gouging.
todo: Look 1–2 weeks ahead in the Market & calendar tab to see which groups an event attracts and whether they match your customers.
Raise prices moderately when demand rises, and make sure you have enough staff.
Don't price more than about 60% above the competitor average in an event week; you risk criticism and lower stars.

prompts.q: Was this week's marketing budget worth it, judging by awareness and RevPAR gains?
why: Marketing builds "awareness", which accumulates and slowly fades: billboards fade slowly, online ads fade fast.
Awareness has diminishing returns: once it is high, the same extra money buys less and less.
A rise in RevPAR may come from the season or an event, not only from marketing.
todo: Compare the extra room revenue with the money spent on marketing in the finance section of the Report tab.
Check awareness in the Customers tab before and after raising the budget.
If your awareness is already above competitors', try cutting the budget and see how fast awareness falls.

lib.title: Event library and how events are drawn
lib.intro: Events follow Faulkner's (2001) tourism crisis management framework: a {disaster} is a sudden change the business cannot control, while a {crisis} is partly caused by the business's own management ({src1}). Multi-week events in the game are strongest in the first week (emergency) and then gradually recover, following the idea of disaster phases ({src2}).
lib.how1: The whole game's event timeline is drawn once at the start from the game code; every hotel in the city gets the same one.
lib.how2: Each week has a {p}% chance of a new event (at most {max} per week).
lib.how3: Events are picked from the library by weight, filtered by city and month, with severity weights at this level: minor ×{minor}, major ×{major}, catastrophic ×{cat}.
lib.how4: Major and catastrophic events happen at most once per game. Some minor events can repeat but need a 4-week gap, and are not drawn again while still active.
lib.how5: Effects are multiplied by this level's severity factor (×{scale}) and fade as the event recovers.
lib.how6: Internal problems are drawn separately for each hotel every week; their chance rises with that hotel's own management.
lib.freqSummary: Simulated {n} games in {city} starting in {month} at the {chaos} level: on average {avg} new events per game (bad {neg} · good {pos})
lib.freqCats: By category: {cats} per game · internal problems are calculated separately during play
lib.freqNote: Bar = approximate chance that the event happens at least once in a game
lib.revealSummary: Answer key: this game's event timeline (for instructors)
lib.revealLabel: Show upcoming emergencies in the calendar (players will see the answers in advance)
lib.seasonSrcTitle: Where the game's seasons come from
lib.seasonSrc: Thai seasons follow {tmd}. Each city's high, shoulder and low seasons are design values based on travel-weather information, e.g. {phuket}, {ranong}; other cities are estimates and should be updated with monthly statistics later.
lib.festivalNote: Festival dates follow {src}. Loy Krathong and Chinese New Year move every year; the game uses approximate dates.
lib.seededTitle: City events (random week, 2–3 announced at the start of the game, {p}% chance of cancellation)

pr.chance: 2% + 8% if last week's reviews were below 3 stars + 4% if understaffed

overbook.chance: 15% if last week's occupancy was above 92%

repair.result: Repair cost {c} ฿, only 6 rooms for sale for 2 weeks

gouging.chance: 30% if your average price is 60% above competitors in an event week

lib.internalNote: Low season is not drawn at random; it follows each city's real seasons in the Market & calendar tab. All effect sizes are design values for learning, not estimates from real data.

final.title: 12 weeks in {city} are over: you placed {rank} of {n}
final.averages: Game averages: Occupancy {occ} · ADR {adr} ฿ · RevPAR {revpar} ฿ · RGI {rgi}
final.rules: Rules: (1) hotels with a cumulative loss always rank below profitable hotels (2) finance score = cumulative profit ÷ best profit in the city × 100, 0 if you lost money (3) reputation comes from stars (4) staff from average satisfaction
debrief: In which weeks was your RGI highest and lowest? Was it driven by MPI or ARI?
How well did you use the event calendar and seasons to price ahead? Did a cancelled event ever hurt you?
Which emergency hit you hardest, and how did you respond in the emergency and recovery phases?
Which bot strategy did best in this city, and which customer groups explain why?
If you only looked at occupancy, where would you misjudge your own performance?
final.debriefNote: Much of the learning from simulation games happens in the debrief ({src}).
final.csvNote: Copy into Excel or Google Sheets for the debrief.

bkk.name: Bangkok
bkk.lm: Temple on the Chao Phraya River
bkk.story: The capital that never sleeps. Business travellers and foreign backpackers come all year, but new places open on every street, so competition is tight.

kkn.name: Khon Kaen
kkn.story: The hub of the northeast (Isan). Conferences and business travellers are the main customers; few foreigners, but busy weekdays.

hkt.name: Phuket
hkt.story: Pearl of the Andaman with a very high share of foreign guests. Nov–Apr is peak season; the southwest monsoon makes May–Oct clearly quieter.

pty.name: Pattaya
pty.story: A beach city close to Bangkok. Thai visitors come at weekends, foreigners all year, with frequent events and sports.

pbi.name: Phetchaburi
pbi.story: An old town below Khao Wang. Thai families stop by at weekends on the way to Cha-am beach; few foreigners, so prices must stay affordable.

rbr.name: Ratchaburi
rbr.story: A town of floating markets and pottery. Thai families and couples often come as day-trippers, so hotels must give them a reason to stay the night.

rng.name: Ranong
rng.story: "Eight months of rain, four of sun." Hot springs and Koh Phayam attract wellness travellers and backpackers, but the May–Oct monsoon is long.

cnx.name: Chiang Mai
cnx.story: The old Lanna city. The cool season is the busiest for Thai and foreign visitors; out of season, nearly half the demand disappears.

pnb.name: Phetchabun
pnb.lm: Sea of mist and cabbage fields
pnb.story: The misty hills of Khao Kho and Phu Thap Boek. Rooms fill very fast in the cool season and the rainy season is quiet: the most seasonal city in the game.

songkran.name: Songkran Festival
songkran.text: 13–15 April: Thais travel and go home at the same time

loykrathong.name: Loy Krathong
loykrathong.text: Full moon of the 12th lunar month, around mid-November (date changes every year)

cny.name: Chinese New Year
cny.text: Late Jan–Feb (date changes every year); hotel demand rises

concert.name: Big concert
concert.text: Young fans and couples book rooms near the venue

conference.name: International conference
conference.text: Companies send staff to attend; business demand jumps

marathon.name: Marathon
marathon.text: Runners and their families stay the night before the race

tradefair.name: Trade fair
tradefair.text: Exhibitors and buyers attend for several days

sport.name: International sports event
sport.text: Foreign sports fans travel to watch

quake.name: Strong earthquake
quake.text: Buildings need safety checks; many tourists cancel.

tsunami.name: Tsunami
tsunami.text: The coast is damaged and unsafe; tourism stops.

flood.name: Major flood
flood.text: Roads are cut off, travel stops and building upkeep costs rise.

storm.name: Storm
storm.text: Heavy rain and strong wind; tourists postpone trips.

pandemic.name: Severe pandemic
pandemic.text: Travel restrictions and local lockdowns; foreign visitors almost disappear.

haze.name: Heavy haze
haze.text: Poor air quality; some tourists avoid the area.

recession.name: Economic downturn
recession.text: People cut travel budgets and become more price-sensitive.

fxstrong.name: Strong baht
fxstrong.text: Thailand looks more expensive to foreigners.

fxweak.name: Weak baht
fxweak.text: Thailand looks better value to foreigners.

energy.name: Energy prices soar
energy.text: Fixed costs rise for every hotel.

protest.name: Violent protests
protest.text: Prolonged rallies; foreigners and business travellers avoid the area.

politics.name: National political crisis
politics.text: A sudden political change (e.g. a coup) hurts travellers' confidence.

advisory.name: Travel advisory
advisory.text: Key source countries tell their citizens to delay travel to this area.

newcomp.name: New competitor hotel opens
newcomp.text: A new hotel (outside the game) opens nearby; customers have more choice permanently.

airbnb.name: More Airbnb-style rentals
airbnb.text: More houses and condos rented by the night take some customers permanently.

labour.name: Service labour shortage
labour.text: Staff at every hotel expect higher pay; satisfaction drops.

viral.name: Viral travel clip about this city
viral.text: Foreign interest in the area rises.

flight.name: New direct flight route
flight.text: Easier travel brings more foreign visitors.

stimulus.name: Domestic tourism stimulus
stimulus.text: The government pays part of hotel costs; more Thais travel.

film.name: Hit series filmed in the city
film.text: Couples and young people visit the filming locations.

pr.name: Reputation crisis
variants: Negative review goes viral on social media
Photos of a dirty room are shared
News of guests falling ill after breakfast

overbook.name: Booking system failure, overbooking
overbook.text: Guests must be moved elsewhere and compensated

repair.name: 2 rooms closed for repair
repair.text: Burst pipe or leaking roof: fewer rooms to sell and repair costs

gouging.name: Criticised for price gouging
gouging.text: Prices far above competitors during an event; guests post complaints

growth.title: Growing the hotel
growth.tier0: Small accommodation (no hotel licence needed) · {rooms} rooms
growth.law: Under Thai law, places with more than 8 rooms or 30 guests need a hotel licence. Type 1 = rooms only, Type 2 = rooms + restaurant ({src}). The game compresses a process that really takes months.
growth.srcLaw: Ministerial Regulation on hotel types, B.E. 2551

growth.step2Info: {cost} ฿ paid when the licence arrives · takes {w} weeks · running cost +{fixed} ฿/week · staff limit {staff}
growth.step3Info: {cost} ฿ · takes {w} weeks · fixed cost +{fixed} ฿/week · needs F&B staff · staff limit {staff}
growth.confirmLicence: Apply for a Type 1 hotel licence? You pay {cost} ฿ this week, and building starts as soon as the licence arrives ({build} ฿ more).
growth.confirmRest: Start the restaurant? You pay {cost} ฿ this week and {fixed} ฿ more fixed cost every week.
